title: Three more heads read through their weights
takeaway: Three further attention heads are shown in the format of Figure 93: five attention snippets on the left, and on the right the top six vocabulary tokens for each of the head's four weight matrices projected through the J-lens. The point the section draws from them is a structural one — heads whose weights project interpretably tend to give similar token rankings across all four matrices — and no function is proposed for any individual head here.
walkthrough:
This is a live widget rather than a static image. It stacks three panels, one for each [[attention-head]], under the labels the authors gave them: "Async error handling", "Temperature" and "Honorific titles". Every panel repeats the layout of Figure 93. Neither the model nor the layer and head index is reported for any of the three.

### The left half: attention

Each panel carries five text snippets of eleven to fifteen tokens, clipped on the left and prefixed with an ellipsis. The last token of every snippet is outlined. That is the query position, and the header above reads "attention pattern from query token" with an arrow pointing down at it. The remaining tokens carry orange shading for the head's attention from that query. The shading runs on a scale from 0 to 1 and saturates at the top, so a fully orange token means the value reached the ramp's ceiling rather than any exact probability.

### The right half: weights read as tokens

Four columns headed $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$ and $W_O$ list six vocabulary tokens each. These are not readouts of activations. Each of the head's weight matrices is composed with the [[jacobian-lens]] and the [[unembedding-matrix]] as $W_U\,J\,W_{\{Q,K,V,O\}}$, which leaves one row per entry of the [[tokenizer-vocabulary]]. Tokens are then ranked by the norm of their row. This is [[weight-vocabulary-projection]] applied to a model component rather than to a [[residual-stream]] activation, the use the paper calls [[component-interpretation]].

### What the three panels show

The async head's four columns are dominated by await, async, promise and try. Its attention runs from a token such as " exception", " catch" or " try" back to the nearest " await" or " async", at 1.0, 0.77, 0.615, 0.415 and 0.403 across the five snippets.

The temperature head reads thermal-quantity words on the query side — temperature, температ, hot, heat, 热 — and specific warm and cold words on the key side and on the value and output sides, which together form the head's [[ov-circuit]]. Its attention does reach " warm", " cooling" and " warming", but often lands harder on neutral neighbours such as " the", " jacket", " average" and " floor".

The honorific head lists Mr, Mrs, Dr and Ms in all four columns. Its attention mostly goes to the immediately preceding title, or stays on the query token itself, so the weight readout carries more of the story than the pattern does.

The section makes one claim about these three, and it is general: many heads with interpretable projections have similar vocabulary rankings across the different weight matrices, which the paper calls somewhat surprising. All three panels fit that description.

terms.definition: The transformer operation that lets a token position pull information from earlier positions. Each head has four weight matrices, and this figure characterises three heads by both what they attend to and what their weights project to in vocabulary space.

The paper's readout technique: a corpus-averaged Jacobian $J$ per layer, which turns a residual-stream direction into scores over the vocabulary via $W_U\,J$. Here it is applied to static weights instead of to an activation.
The label the authors give the first head. It is a name assigned from the head's behaviour, not a quantity the widget computes.
The label for the second head, whose query-side tokens are words for thermal quantity and whose key, value and output tokens are specific warm and cold words.
The label for the third head, whose four weight matrices all rank English personal titles at the top.
The header over the left half of each panel, with a downward arrow at its right end pointing at the outlined final token. It states that the shading is attention measured from that one position.
The header over the right half of each panel. It states that the four columns below are vocabulary tokens ranked by J-lens projection of the head's weight matrices.
The final token of each snippet, drawn with a thin box. The whole shading row is the attention distribution computed from this position back over the snippet.
One short passage of text, shown as a single line of tokens. Each is clipped on the left with a leading ellipsis so the query token sits flush at the right edge.
The colour ramp on each token: white at zero attention, full orange at the ceiling. Orange is reserved throughout the paper for activation or attention strength.
The head's query projection. Its column lists the tokens whose J-lens directions couple most strongly into the query subspace, that is, what content at the current position makes the head fire.
The head's key projection. Its column lists the tokens whose J-lens directions the head most strongly looks for at earlier positions.
The head's value projection: what the head picks up from the position it attends to. Together with $W_O$ it forms the head's OV circuit.
The head's output projection, which writes the attended content back into the residual stream. Its column lists the tokens that write-back most strongly promotes.
The unembedding matrix, the model's final linear map from residual-stream vectors to vocabulary scores. It is the left factor of the composition used here.
The layer's corpus-averaged Jacobian, the matrix at the centre of the J-lens. Composing $W_U\,J$ gives the linear map from a residual direction to vocabulary scores.

The composition ranked in the right half: one of the head's four weight matrices, pushed through the Jacobian and the unembedding. The result has one row per vocabulary token, and tokens are ordered by the norm of their row.
The rule that picks the six tokens in each column. A large row norm means that token's lens direction has a large component in whatever subspace that weight matrix reads from or writes to.
The running per-position vector that all four of a head's matrices read from or write to, and the space in which J-lens vectors live.
The fixed token set the ranking runs over. Because leading spaces and capitalisation make separate entries, a column can list what looks like the same word twice, for example async and " async".

A token at the top of the async head's query, key and output columns, and the token most snippets attend to. In JavaScript it marks the point where a promise is waited on and where an error can surface.
Case variants of the same word appearing across all four of the first head's columns. They are separate vocabulary entries, which is why the word repeats within a column.
A word fragment in the async head's query column: the opening piece of "await" under a different tokenization.
The sixth token in the async head's query column, and the only one there that names the failure rather than the awaiting construct.
Tokens in the async head's key, value and output columns. A promise is the JavaScript object an await suspends on, and a rejected one is what becomes an exception.
A token in the async head's value column, and the query token of one snippet. It opens the block that catches the exception.
Case variants heading the temperature head's query column, and its top output token. Most of that head's snippets end on this word as the query.
A Russian fragment, the opening of температура (temperature). It appears in the temperature head's query, key and output columns, so the head's reading is not confined to English.
Two further thermal-quantity tokens in the temperature head's query and output columns. Both also occur as query tokens in the snippets.
A Chinese character meaning hot or heat, in the temperature head's query and output columns. Another sign the head's readout spans scripts.

The top tokens of the temperature head's key and value columns. They are specific thermal values rather than the quantity word, which is what separates the key and value sides from the query side here.
Further specific thermal tokens on the temperature head's key and value sides. The same words appear as attended tokens inside the snippets.
A Russian fragment, the opening of холодный (cold), in the temperature head's value column.
The top token of every column of the honorific head, in both capitalisations. Also the query token of one snippet.
The other titles filling the honorific head's four columns. All four columns list the same small set in slightly different orders.
A title appearing only in the honorific head's key column, not in the other three.
The sixth token in the honorific head's key column. It is the abbreviation for Saint or Street, and the one entry there that is not a personal title.
The general move this figure instances: projecting a static weight direction, rather than an activation, through the lens to read what the component handles.

numbers.meaning: The figure's number in the paper. It sits in appendix section 10.24.3, on interpreting model components with the J-lens.
The figure whose format is reused here. Figure 93 shows one head, the "British spelling to Commonwealth nationality" head, with the same two-half layout.
The number of heads shown, stacked as three panels. The section calls them three more examples beyond the one worked through in Figure 93.
The weight matrices per head: query, key, value and output. Four is fixed by the transformer's attention design, not chosen by the authors.
Tokens listed per column, so 24 per head and 72 in the figure. The cut-off is a display choice; the ranking itself runs over the whole vocabulary.
Snippets per head, so 15 attention rows in total. Each snippet is a separate context in which the head was run.
The token length of a snippet. The range comes from clipping each example to a fixed display width, which lands on a whole-token boundary at a different count each time.
The range of the shading weight on each token, mapped from white to full orange. Values are clipped into this range for display, so 1 marks the ceiling rather than a probability of one.

A saturated token. It occurs on " await" in the first async snippet, on " temperature" and on both " floor" and " hot" in temperature snippets, and on " Mr" and " Mrs" in honorific snippets. Two tokens both at 1.0 in one row show the values are not a normalised distribution.
The async head's weight on the token it attends to most in each of its five snippets, in order. Four of the five peaks fall on " await"; the fourth falls on " async".

The weight on " out" in the first async snippet, the second-highest there. It is part of "the await times out", so the head spreads some weight across the failing construct rather than onto " await" alone.
The async head's weight on its own query token in each snippet. These are low, which is what makes the head read as retrieving from an earlier position rather than sitting on the current one.
The temperature head's weight on its own query token across the five snippets. Two saturate and two are low, so the head's self-weight is not consistent.

The temperature head's weight on the specific thermal word in each snippet: " warm", " cooling", " warming", " warm" and " warm". These are the tokens its key and value columns predict it should find.

Weights on non-thermal neighbours in the temperature snippets: " the", " jacket", " average" and " floor". Each exceeds the thermal word in its own snippet, so the attention pattern is looser than the weight readout suggests.
The honorific head's weight on the preceding title in each snippet: " Mr", " Dr", " Dr", " Mrs" and " Ms". The last two are small because the query token in those snippets is itself a title.

The honorific head's weight on its own query token. It is substantial in every snippet and saturates in the two where the query is a title, which is the main reason the pattern reads less cleanly than the four columns do.
The typical background weight on the scene-setting tokens at the left of each snippet. It renders as near-white and marks the part of the context the head ignores.
